chapter_title: Designing an A/B Test with Students
learning_objective: The learner will compare how three assignment methods balance two groups of 12 students on their pre-test averages, and answer 4 of 4 questions about the methods, with at least 3 of 4 correct on the first attempt.
specification:
Type: microsim **sim-id:** group-assignment-lab
**Library:** p5.js
**Status:** Specified
**Bloom Level:** Analyze
**Bloom Verb:** compare
**Learning Objective:** The learner will compare how three assignment methods balance two groups of 12 students on their pre-test averages, and answer 4 of 4 questions about the methods, with at least 3 of 4 correct on the first attempt. **Prerequisites:** Random Assignment, Pre-Test, Control Group, Treatment Group (all defined in this chapter above this block). **Evidence of Mastery:** The learner answers four questions after running the methods. An answer is correct when it matches the Correct answer column in Content. Mastery is at least 3 of 4 correct on the first attempt. Running the methods is exploration, not evidence. **Misconceptions:** (1) Random assignment always gives equal groups. (2) Letting students choose is fair because it respects their preferences. (3) Blocked assignment can be done before the pre-test. **Instructional Rationale:** Comparing methods on the same class is an Analyze-level action. Running each method many times shows that random assignment works on average, varies from run to run, and is improved by blocking. **Content:** The class: 24 students with these made-up pre-test scores, out of 100: 22, 28, 31, 35, 38, 41, 43, 45, 47, 48, 50, 52, 53, 55, 57, 58, 60, 62, 64, 66, 68, 70, 74, 78. The average of all 24 is 51.875. The three methods: | Method | What the sim does | |---|---| | Students choose | The 12 highest scores form the improved group and the 12 lowest form the original group. Every press gives the same result. | | Simple random assignment | Each press forms two groups of 12 by a fresh random shuffle of the 24 students. | | Blocked random assignment | The sim sorts the scores, pairs neighbors (22 with 28, 31 with 35, and so on up to 74 with 78), and decides by a fresh coin flip within each pair which student goes to each group. | For every press the sim shows the two group averages and the absolute difference between them, and keeps a running list of the differences for each method. Facts shown after at least 20 presses of a method, from 20,000 simulated assignments of this class: | Method | Difference between group averages | |---|---| | Students choose | 23.75 points: group averages of 63.75 and 40.0 | | Simple random assignment | Median 4.25; 95 percent of splits are <= 11.9; 42 percent of splits are > 5 | | Blocked random assignment | Median 0.58; 95 percent of splits are <= 1.6; the largest is 2.6 | The four questions: | # | Question | Choices | Correct answer | Why (shown as feedback) | |---|---|---|---|---| | 1 | Which method builds the largest imbalance into the groups? | Students choose; Simple random assignment; Blocked random assignment | Students choose | The 12 highest scorers form one group, so the averages differ by 23.75. | | 2 | Does simple random assignment guarantee equal pre-test averages? | Yes; No | No | Some splits differ by more than 5 points. | | 3 | What must you know before you can use blocked random assignment? | The post-test scores; Each student's pre-test score; The teacher's preference | Each student's pre-test score | The scores are needed to sort and pair the students. | | 4 | Which method gave the smallest typical difference? | Students choose; Simple random assignment; Blocked random assignment | Blocked random assignment | Its median difference is 0.58. | **Provenance:** The scores are made up for this chapter, and the sim labels them "illustrative examples". The simulated figures were computed for this class from 20,000 random assignments with a fixed seed, and the sim labels them "simulation results for this class". **Rules:** The group sizes are always 12 and 12. A press never changes the class. The facts appear only after at least 20 presses of the method, so that the learner sees the spread before reading the summary. **Learner Activity:** 1. The learner picks a method and presses Form groups at least 20 times for each random method. 2. After each press the learner sees the two averages and their difference. 3. The learner presses Quiz and answers the four questions. 4. After question 4 the sim shows the summary. **Feedback:** 4 questions in the order of the table, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: [answer]. [Why]". Incorrect: "Not quite. The answer is [answer]. [Why]". The summary shows "[n] of 4 correct on the first attempt". At 3 or more it adds "You can compare ways to form groups." Below 3 it lists the Why text of each missed question. **Starting State:** The class table, the Students choose method selected, and no presses yet. **Chapter Anchors:** The chapter's table of three methods uses the same class and the same figures as this sim.
